newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Multinational force set for lawless Albania.
newsitem.headline: Multinational force set for lawless Albania.

text.p: Random violence gripped Albania on Saturday while Italy prepared a multinational security force to protect humanitarian relief operations in the lawless Balkan country.
Armed outlaw gangs were reported to have killed six people last night in attacks from the northern border town of Shkoder to the southern Adriatic port of Vlore.
Masked gunmen near the Greek border held up a bus coming into Albania near the village of Grapsh, seizing possessions but leaving about 30 passengers unharmed on Friday, police said.

Violence has raged in Albania since an armed insurrection in the south this month. Rebel councils now control many towns, demanding President Sali Berisha resign, and outlaw gangs roam the countryside terrorising villagers.
The anarchy has disrupted food and medicine, prompting the U.N. Security Council to approve an Italian-led multinational security force to protect humanitarian relief operations.
Italy's ambassador to the United Nations, Paulo Fulci, said such a protection force and relief operations had risks "but if you feed the people they are less nervous on an empty stomach".
Albania's European Union neighbours -- Italy and Greece -- have been concerned that the lawlessness gripping the country could trigger a wave of illegal immigrants.

Some 13,000 people have fled already across the Adriatic to Italy since March 13, and an unknown number of Albanian refugees died on Friday night when their boat capsized and sank after a collision with an Italian navy ship.

Fulci said Albania had about a week of food left. There has been no sign of malnutrition but the Red Cross has warned that a collapse of the food distribution system could threaten about 10 percent of the 3.4 million population.

The U.N. resolution approved the force for three months, which means it will be in place during national elections due in June. Berisha agreed to the vote, three years early, and named an all-party government this month to try to weather the crisis.

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino welcomed the U.N. decision, saying: "It was good this resolution was approved in record time and it is the wish of the Albanian government that these forces arrive very soon."

The U.N. resolution approved the force's right to shoot in self-defence and said participating states would foot the bill. Italy has said it expected to deploy 2,500 international troops or police, mostly from EU countries.
Military experts from Italy, France, Greece, Spain, Austria and Portugal have been in Albania for the past week to scout the terrain. Turkey and Romania also want to join the force.

Diplomats in Tirana said much of the groundwork had been done and Italy, which has been keen to deploy the force for some time, could now move quickly. Advance contingents could arrive next week, some EU diplomats said.
The multinational protection force will be deployed around the main Adriatic ports of Durres and Vlore, scene of some of the worst violence in the popular uprising against Berisha.
It will also protect the Tirana airport and be in charge of ensuring the safety of humanitarian aid convoys distributing food and medical supplies around the country.
The greatest danger to the Italian-led force will be in the countryside, where outlaw gangs have roamed with impunity since the insurrection against Berisha early this month.

The gangs, along with thousands of Albanians, looted army weapons depots, stealing thousands of firearms. The gangs have imposed a reign of terror in many parts of the countryside, robbing banks, looting companies and taking what they want.

Gunmen killed five people in the northern town of Shkoder on Friday night and one person in the southern town of Vlore, the state ATA news agency reported. Three people also died in accidents with nearly acquired arms in the town of Berat.
